text: To understand the trucks, you have to start with a scooter.
Gorakhpur, nineteen seventy-eight.
A young man named Subrata Roy starts a small savings business. The stories say he had two thousand rupees, a borrowed scooter, and one desk.
His idea is simple.
Millions of Indians have no bank account. They earn a little every day, in cash.
So Sahara sends people to them.
Meet Kamla. She's our example: not a real person, but someone like millions who were.
She sells vegetables. Every evening, a man from Sahara stops at her stall.
Twenty rupees today. Thirty tomorrow. He writes it in a little book.
He knows her name. He knows her children's names.
He's not a banker in a tie. He's from the neighbourhood.
And he tells her she's part of something bigger. A family.
Sahara calls itself exactly that: the Sahara India Pariwar. The Sahara family.
And the family grows. And grows.
An airline. Television channels. Townships. A private hill city outside Pune.
The name goes on the shirts of the Indian cricket team.
Hotels in London and New York.
Subrata Roy becomes "Saharasri". He lives like a king, and he says the family comes first.
And for years, nobody asks the simple question.
Where does all this money come from?
Kamla doesn't ask either. Why would she?
Her book says her money is there. The man comes every evening.
But in a different office, far from her stall, someone is about to read the fine print.
